newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Top lawmakers say Russia budget likely to pass.
newsitem.headline: Top lawmakers say Russia budget likely to pass.

text.p: Top Russian lawmakers said the 1997 draft budget, once rejected and once postponed, is likely to be approved on Sunday, but only after firey debate.

"Of course the fight will be hot, but probably the decision will be positive," the Communist speaker of the State Duma lower house of parliament, Gennady Seleznyov said on Saturday after the Duma budget committee voted 15:7 in favor of the plan.
Communists, the dominant party in the Duma, called for the rejection of the budget during the previous debate on December 6, when voting on the first reading was postponed until Sunday.
"The state is bankrupt, the president is ill, the government is helpless and the Duma is powerless," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov said at the time.

Zyuganov did not comment on Saturday, but Interfax news agency quoted Nikolai Kharintonov, head of Communist-allied Agrarian Party, as saying most of his bloc would support the budget, which must pass three readings.
Ultra-nationalist LDPR party leader Vladimir Zhirinovsky made a surprise about-face to support the budget on December 6.
Interfax quoted the head of the liberal opposition Yabloko party Grigory Yavlinsky as saying his party would vote against the budget. This could make it the only major party to oppose the bill.
Yabloko member Mikhail Zadornov, head of the budget committee, predicted on Tuesday the draft would pass.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who celebrated four years at his post on Saturday, offered an olive branch to the Duma in his December 6 speech, before the Duma postponed the vote.
He unexpectedly called for the creation of an off-budget investment fund, a "budget of growth" to lure foreign funds, partly thanks to government guarantees of commercial loans.
The Duma has repeatedly called for increased government investment in industry in order to revive growth.
On Tuesday Chernomyrdin promised to pay wage arrears of some 7.9 trillion roubles ($1.43 billion) this month.

"In all main spheres, except the army, 100 percent of debts will be repaid in December. This way we will make our debts disappear and will not allow new indebtedness to form and grow," he said, without specifying funding sources.
But Chernomyrdin also told the Duma Russia would not print new money to cover a wider budget deficit wider than 3.5 percent of gross domestic product, as called for by some communists.
If deputies fail to approve a budget by year-end, Russia will have to use interim budgets or re-use the 1996 plan.

But fears that failure to pass the budget on Sunday, a working day in Russia, could further jeopardise monthly payouts of a $10 billion International Monetary Fund loan, were eased when the IMF approved disbursement of a delayed tranche.
It gave the go-ahead on Friday for the release of roughly $336 million, citing "improved revenue performance". It had previously criticised Russia's tax collection record.
The Russian government has championed a tight monetary policy which has led to steep falls in inflation, from close to 20 percent in January 1995 to 1.9 percent in November.
But the squeeze has also contributed to misery for millions of workers, who have not been paid for months by cash-strapped firms. Tax revenue, in turn, is well below target.

Chernomyrdin told the Duma that if budget targets were met and 1997 inflation did not exceed 11-12 percent, the economy could grow by two percent. GDP fell six percent in real terms in the first 10 months of this year from January-October 1995.
The target deficit had been widened from the government's initial proposal of 3.3 percent and Chernomyrdin said a further widening of the gap could be damaging.
"We must not allow this to happen. If we do, all our sufferings and pains will be in vain," he said. ($1=5541 Rouble)
